data.name: Old Fashioned
data.description: Whiskey, a little sugar and bitters, stirred and poured over a big cube. The drink every bartender should nail.
steps: Add syrup and bitters to a mixing glass.
Add whiskey and ice. Stir 20–30 seconds.
Strain over a large cube.
Express an orange peel over the top and drop it in.
data.tasteLine: Strong and smooth. Basically whiskey, seasoned.
data.spiritLine: The whiskey is the star. A higher-proof bourbon, or a spicy rye, stands up to the sugar and bitters.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “An Old Fashioned: whiskey, a little sugar and bitters, with an orange peel. Bourbon or rye?”
data.story: One of the oldest cocktails. In the early 1800s a “cocktail” meant spirit, sugar, water and bitters. As drinks got fancier, guests asked for whiskey cocktails made “the old-fashioned way,” and the name stuck.

video.title: How I Make an Old Fashioned · Anders Erickson

data.name: Manhattan
data.description: Rye whiskey and sweet vermouth with bitters, stirred and served up with a cherry. Rich and elegant.
steps: Chill the glass.
Stir everything with ice for about 30 seconds.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Garnish with a brandied cherry.
data.tasteLine: Smooth, rich and a little sweet.
data.spiritLine: Rye’s spice balances the sweet vermouth. That’s why it’s the classic choice.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Manhattan: rye, sweet vermouth and bitters, served up with a cherry.”
data.story: Born in New York in the 1870s or 1880s. A popular story ties it to the Manhattan Club, but nobody knows for sure. It was one of the first cocktails made with vermouth.

video.title: How to Make a Manhattan · Anders Erickson

data.name: Martini
data.description: Gin and dry vermouth, stirred ice-cold and served up with a twist or olives. Simple, so every detail matters.
steps: Chill the glass.
Stir with ice for about 30 seconds, until very cold.
Strain into the chilled glass.
Twist or olives, as the guest asked.
data.tasteLine: Clean, cold and bracing.
data.spiritLine: A London Dry gin gives the classic crisp, juniper bite.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “Gin or vodka? Olives or a twist?” Always ask both.
data.story: The Martini grew out of sweeter gin-and-vermouth drinks in the late 1800s. Through the 1900s it got drier and drier, and James Bond made “shaken, not stirred” famous.

video.title: How to make a Martini · Anders Erickson

data.name: Negroni
data.description: Gin, Campari and sweet vermouth in equal parts, stirred over ice. Bitter, bold and a classic before dinner.
steps: Stir everything with ice for about 20 seconds.
Strain over a large cube.
Express an orange peel over the top.
data.tasteLine: Bitter first, then sweet and herbal.

riffs.name: Americano
riffs.note: Campari and vermouth with soda, no gin.

data.spiritLine: Campari gives the Negroni its red color and its bitter backbone.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Negroni: gin, Campari and sweet vermouth. Bitter and bold.”
data.story: Legend says Count Camillo Negroni asked for gin instead of soda in his Americano, in Florence around 1919. It became Italy’s classic before-dinner drink.

video.title: The Negroni and the Americano · Anders Erickson

data.name: Boulevardier
data.description: A Negroni made with bourbon or rye instead of gin. Richer and warmer, great for fall and winter.
steps: Stir everything with ice for about 20 seconds.
Strain over a large cube, or up into a coupe.
Express an orange peel over the top.
data.tasteLine: Bittersweet and warming.
data.spiritLine: Bourbon makes it rounder and sweeter than a Negroni.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Boulevardier is a Negroni made with whiskey. Richer and warmer.”
data.story: Named after Boulevardier, a magazine for Americans in Paris. It first appeared in a 1927 bar book from Harry’s New York Bar in Paris.

video.title: The Boulevardier · Anders Erickson

data.name: Sazerac
data.description: Rye, sugar and Peychaud’s bitters in a glass rinsed with absinthe. Served cold with no ice.
steps: Rinse a chilled rocks glass with absinthe and dump the extra.
Stir rye, syrup and bitters with ice.
Strain into the glass, no ice.
Express a lemon peel over the top, then discard it.
data.tasteLine: Aromatic and strong, with a hint of licorice.
data.spiritLine: Rye was the New Orleans standard: spicy and bold.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Sazerac: rye, Peychaud’s bitters and an absinthe rinse. Strong and aromatic.”
data.story: Named after Sazerac cognac, its original base in 1800s New Orleans. Rye took over later. Today it’s the official cocktail of New Orleans.

video.title: The Sazerac Cocktail · Anders Erickson

data.name: Margarita
data.description: Tequila, fresh lime and orange liqueur, shaken and served on the rocks or up, usually with salt.
steps: Salt the rim if the guest wants it (half rim is a nice option).
Shake everything hard with ice.
Strain over fresh ice, or up.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
data.tasteLine: Tart, bright and refreshing.

riffs.name: Tommy’s Margarita
riffs.note: Agave syrup instead of orange liqueur.

data.spiritLine: A 100% agave blanco keeps it bright and peppery.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “Salt, no salt, or half? Rocks or up?”
data.story: Several bartenders in Mexico and the US claimed to invent it in the 1930s and 40s. Nobody knows for sure. Today it’s one of the most popular cocktails in America.

video.title: 5 ways to make a Margarita · Anders Erickson

data.name: Daiquiri
data.description: Rum, fresh lime and sugar, shaken and served up. Not the frozen kind: the classic is three ingredients, perfectly balanced.
steps: Shake hard with ice for 10–12 seconds.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
data.tasteLine: The perfect sour.
data.spiritLine: A clean white rum lets the lime shine.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A classic daiquiri: rum, lime and sugar, shaken and served up.”
data.story: Named after a beach near Santiago de Cuba, where Americans mixed rum, lime and sugar around 1900. Hemingway helped make the Havana daiquiri famous.

video.title: The Daiquiri · Anders Erickson

data.name: Whiskey Sour
data.description: Bourbon, lemon and sugar, often shaken with egg white for a silky foam topped with bitters.
steps: Shake everything without ice first (dry shake) to build the foam.
Add ice and shake again.
Strain over fresh ice.
Add 3 drops of bitters on the foam and a cherry.
data.tasteLine: Tart, round and silky.

riffs.name: New York Sour
riffs.note: A red wine float on top.

riffs.name: Gold Rush
riffs.note: Honey instead of sugar, no egg.

data.spiritLine: Bourbon’s vanilla and caramel round out the lemon.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A whiskey sour, made with egg white for a silky foam. With or without egg?”
data.story: Sours go back to sailors mixing spirits with citrus. The Whiskey Sour was in print by the 1860s, and egg white foam is the classic option.

video.title: How to Make the Best Whiskey Sour · Anders Erickson

data.allergyNote: Egg white is raw and optional. Ask every guest, and note it on the ticket.

data.name: Gimlet
data.description: Gin, fresh lime and sugar, shaken and served up. Crisp and bright.
steps: Shake hard with ice.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with a lime wheel.
data.tasteLine: Clean, tart and refreshing.
data.spiritLine: Gin’s botanicals meet bright lime.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A gimlet: gin and lime, shaken and served up. Crisp and tart.”
data.story: British sailors drank gin with lime cordial; the lime helped prevent scurvy. The Gimlet grew from that habit.

data.name: Cosmopolitan
data.description: Citrus vodka, orange liqueur, lime and a splash of cranberry, shaken and served up. Tart, not sweet.
steps: Shake hard with ice.
Double strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish with an orange peel or lime wheel.
data.tasteLine: Tart, bright and a little fruity.
data.spiritLine: Citrus vodka adds lemon zest under the cranberry.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Cosmo: citrus vodka, orange liqueur, lime and a splash of cranberry. Tart, not sweet.”
data.story: Bartender Toby Cecchini is credited with the modern Cosmo, in New York in 1988. Sex and the City made it famous in the late 1990s.

data.name: Last Word
data.description: Equal parts gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino liqueur and lime. Herbal, tart and a little sweet.
steps: Shake hard with ice.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
Serve without a garnish, or with a cherry.
data.tasteLine: Herbal, bright and perfectly balanced.

riffs.name: Naked & Famous
riffs.note: Mezcal, Aperol, Yellow Chartreuse and lime.

data.spiritLine: Chartreuse is the soul of the drink: 130 herbs in one bottle.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Last Word: equal parts gin, Green Chartreuse, maraschino and lime. It was created right here in Detroit.”
data.story: Created at the Detroit Athletic Club around 1916. It was nearly forgotten until a Seattle bartender brought it back in the early 2000s. A Detroit original.

video.title: How to Make a Last Word · Anders Erickson

data.name: Paper Plane
data.description: Equal parts bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino and lemon. Bittersweet, bright and easy to love.
steps: Shake hard with ice.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
No garnish needed.
data.tasteLine: Bittersweet and balanced.
data.spiritLine: Nonino adds orange and a gentle bittersweet depth.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Paper Plane: bourbon, Aperol, Amaro Nonino and lemon. Bittersweet and bright.”
data.story: Bartender Sam Ross created it in 2007 and named it after the M.I.A. song Paper Planes. It’s a modern classic built on equal parts.

data.name: Penicillin
data.description: Blended Scotch, lemon and honey-ginger syrup, with a float of smoky Islay Scotch on top.
steps: Shake the Scotch, lemon and syrup with ice.
Strain over a large cube.
Gently float the Islay Scotch on top.
Garnish with candied ginger.
data.tasteLine: Sweet, spicy and smoky.
data.spiritLine: The smoky Islay float is the drink’s signature.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Penicillin: Scotch with honey, ginger and lemon, and a smoky float on top.”
data.story: Sam Ross created it at Milk & Honey in New York in 2005. It became one of the most copied modern classics.

data.name: Espresso Martini
data.description: Vodka, fresh espresso and coffee liqueur, shaken hard for a thick, creamy foam.
steps: Pull a fresh shot of espresso.
Shake everything very hard with ice to build the foam.
Double strain into a chilled glass.
Float three coffee beans on top.
data.tasteLine: Rich, smooth and wide awake.
data.spiritLine: Vodka stays out of the way so the coffee leads.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “An Espresso Martini: vodka, fresh espresso and coffee liqueur, shaken to a creamy foam.”
data.story: London bartender Dick Bradsell created it in the 1980s, when a guest asked for a drink to wake her up.

data.name: Sidecar
data.description: Cognac, orange liqueur and fresh lemon, shaken and served up, often with a sugared rim. The brandy sour every bartender should know.
steps: Sugar half the rim of a chilled coupe, if the guest wants it.
Shake cognac, orange liqueur and lemon hard with ice for 10–12 seconds.
Double strain into the coupe and garnish with an orange twist.
data.tasteLine: Bright and tart, with brandy warmth underneath.

riffs.name: Between the Sheets
riffs.note: Splits the base with light rum.

riffs.name: Brandy Crusta
riffs.note: The older New Orleans cousin, with a full sugar rim.

data.spiritLine: A VS or VSOP cognac gives the drink body and a little oak against the lemon.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Sidecar: cognac, orange liqueur and lemon, shaken and served up. Bright, with a little brandy warmth.”
data.story: Usually traced to Paris or London just after World War I. The popular story says it was named for a customer who rode to the bar in a motorcycle sidecar. Nobody knows for sure.

video.title: How I Make a Sidecar · Anders Erickson

data.name: Pisco Sour
data.description: Pisco, fresh lime, sugar and egg white, shaken into a silky foam and finished with drops of bitters. Peru calls it the national drink, and Chile claims it too.
steps: Shake pisco, lime, syrup and egg white without ice first, to build the foam.
Add ice and shake hard again.
Double strain into a chilled coupe and dot the foam with 3 drops of bitters.
data.tasteLine: Tart and bright, with a soft, creamy foam. Tell guests it has raw egg white.

riffs.name: Chilean Pisco Sour
riffs.note: Chilean pisco, often with lemon and no bitters.

data.spiritLine: A grape brandy from Peru and Chile. Its floral fruit is what makes this sour different.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Pisco Sour: pisco, lime and a silky egg-white foam with a few drops of bitters. It does have raw egg white.”
data.story: Usually credited to Victor Morris, an American who ran a bar in Lima, Peru, around the 1920s. Peru and Chile both call the drink their own.

video.title: The Pisco Sour · Anders Erickson

data.allergyNote: Egg white is raw. Ask every guest, and note it on the ticket.

data.name: Paloma
data.description: Tequila, lime and grapefruit soda over ice, with a pinch of salt. Easy and refreshing.
steps: Salt the rim if the guest wants it.
Add tequila, lime and salt to a glass full of ice.
Top with grapefruit soda.
Stir gently and garnish.
data.tasteLine: Bright, bubbly and easy.
data.spiritLine: Blanco tequila keeps it light and bright.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Paloma: tequila and grapefruit soda with lime. Light and refreshing.”
data.story: Its origin is unclear, but it’s a favorite across Mexico, usually made with grapefruit soda.

video.title: The Paloma: Mexico's National Cocktail · Anders Erickson

data.name: Moscow Mule
data.description: Vodka, lime and spicy ginger beer, served in a copper mug over ice.
steps: Fill the mug with ice.
Add vodka and lime.
Top with ginger beer and stir gently.
Garnish with a lime wedge.
data.tasteLine: Spicy, tart and fizzy.
data.spiritLine: Vodka lets the spicy ginger beer lead.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Moscow Mule: vodka, lime and ginger beer, in a copper mug.”
data.story: Created in Los Angeles in the 1940s to help sell vodka and ginger beer to Americans. The copper mug was part of the pitch.

data.name: Mojito
data.description: White rum, fresh mint, lime and sugar over crushed ice, topped with soda.
steps: Gently press the mint with syrup and lime. Don’t shred it.
Add rum and crushed ice.
Top with soda and stir up from the bottom.
Clap a mint sprig to wake it up and garnish.
data.tasteLine: Cool, minty and refreshing.

riffs.name: Southside
riffs.note: Gin, mint and lime, served up.

riffs.name: Old Cuban
riffs.note: Aged rum, bitters and Champagne, served up.

data.spiritLine: A light white rum keeps it fresh and minty.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Mojito: rum, fresh mint and lime with soda. Cool and refreshing.”
data.story: From Cuba, where an older drink of rum, lime, sugar and mint was popular. Havana’s bars made the Mojito world famous.

video.title: Two Ways To Make A Mojito · Anders Erickson

data.name: Aperol Spritz
data.description: Prosecco, Aperol and a splash of soda over ice. Light, bittersweet and made for before dinner.
steps: Fill a wine glass with ice.
Add prosecco first, then Aperol, so it mixes.
Add a splash of soda.
Garnish with an orange slice.
data.tasteLine: Light, bubbly and bittersweet.
data.spiritLine: Aperol brings the orange glow and gentle bitterness.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “An Aperol Spritz: prosecco and Aperol with soda. Light and bittersweet.”
data.story: Spritzes go back to the 1800s, when Austrian soldiers in the Veneto added a splash of water to local wine. Aperol was created in Padua in 1919.

data.name: French 75
data.description: Gin, lemon and sugar, shaken and topped with Champagne. Bright, bubbly and elegant.
steps: Shake gin, lemon and syrup with ice.
Strain into a flute.
Top slowly with Champagne.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
data.tasteLine: Celebratory and crisp.
data.spiritLine: Dry Champagne gives it lift and bubbles.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A French 75: gin, lemon and Champagne. Bright and bubbly.”
data.story: Named after the French 75mm field gun from World War I, because the drink packs a punch.

video.title: How to make a French 75 · Anders Erickson

data.name: Lemon Drop
data.description: Vodka, fresh lemon and orange liqueur, shaken and served up in a sugar-rimmed glass. Sweet, tart and easy.
steps: Rim a chilled glass with sugar.
Shake vodka, lemon, orange liqueur and syrup hard with ice.
Strain into the glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
data.tasteLine: Sweet and tart, like a lemon candy.

riffs.name: Raspberry Lemon Drop
riffs.note: Add raspberry liqueur or muddled raspberries.

riffs.name: Lemon Drop Shot
riffs.note: Same build, served as a shot with a sugared lemon wedge.

data.spiritLine: A clean vodka lets the lemon lead.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Lemon Drop: vodka, lemon and orange liqueur, shaken and served in a sugar-rimmed glass. Sweet and tart.”
data.story: Usually credited to Henry Africa’s, a San Francisco bar, in the 1970s. Bar lead to check the history.

data.name: Rob Roy
data.description: Blended Scotch, sweet vermouth and bitters, stirred and served up with a cherry.
steps: Add Scotch, vermouth and bitters to a mixing glass.
Add ice and stir until well chilled.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Express an orange peel over the top, discard it, and add a cherry.
data.tasteLine: Like a Manhattan, but rounder and a little malty.
data.spiritLine: A blended Scotch keeps it smooth. A smoky Islay changes the drink completely, so ask first.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Rob Roy is a Manhattan made with Scotch: sweet vermouth, bitters and a cherry.”
data.story: Named after the Rob Roy operetta, which opened on Broadway in 1894. It was likely created at the nearby Waldorf Astoria as a Scotch take on the Manhattan.

video.title: Master The Classics: Rob Roy · The Educated Barfly

data.name: Vieux Carré
data.description: Rye, cognac and sweet vermouth with a little Bénédictine and two kinds of bitters. Rich, spicy and smooth.
steps: Add everything to a mixing glass.
Add ice and stir well.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish with orange zest and a cherry.
data.tasteLine: Rich and layered: spicy rye, soft cognac and herbal honey.
data.spiritLine: Two bases share the work: rye brings spice, cognac brings fruit and softness.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Vieux Carré is a New Orleans classic: rye, cognac and sweet vermouth with a touch of herbal liqueur. Rich and smooth.”
data.story: Created in 1938 by Walter Bergeron, head bartender at what is now the Carousel Bar in New Orleans’ Hotel Monteleone. The name is French for the French Quarter: the “old square.”

video.title: How to Make a Vieux Carré AKA the "Old Square" · Anders Erickson

data.name: Rusty Nail
data.description: Scotch and Drambuie, a honeyed Scotch liqueur, over ice. Two ingredients, very strong, a little sweet.
steps: Fill a rocks glass with ice.
Pour in the Scotch and Drambuie.
Stir gently.
Garnish with lemon zest.
data.tasteLine: Strong and warming, with honey and herbs.
data.spiritLine: Blended Scotch is the usual choice. The ratio can run from 1:1 to 2:1, so check how the guest likes it.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Rusty Nail is Scotch and Drambuie, a honey Scotch liqueur, over ice.”
data.story: Scotch and Drambuie first show up together in 1937 as the B.I.F., after the British Industries Fair. The 21 Club in New York made it popular as the Rusty Nail, and the Rat Pack made it their drink.

video.title: How to Make a Rusty Nail - strong and sweet · Anders Erickson

data.name: Vesper
data.description: Gin and vodka with a little Lillet Blanc, shaken cold and served up with a lemon twist.
steps: Add gin, vodka and Lillet to a shaker.
Shake with ice until very cold.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish with a lemon twist.
data.tasteLine: Bone-dry and very cold, with a bright lemon finish.
data.spiritLine: Gin leads, vodka softens it. Lillet Blanc stands in for Kina Lillet, which isn’t made any more.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Vesper is James Bond’s martini: gin, vodka and Lillet, shaken, with a lemon twist.”
data.story: Ian Fleming created it in his first James Bond novel, Casino Royale (1953). Bond orders three measures of Gordon’s, one of vodka and half a measure of Kina Lillet, shaken, and names it after Vesper Lynd.

video.title: How to make a better VESPER than James Bond himself · Anders Erickson

data.name: Oaxaca Old Fashioned
data.tagline: Tequila and mezcal, the old-fashioned way
data.description: Reposado tequila and a little smoky mezcal, sweetened with agave and seasoned with bitters, over a big cube.
steps: Add everything to a mixing glass.
Add ice and stir.
Strain over a large cube.
Flame an orange zest over the top and drop it in.
data.tasteLine: Smooth tequila with a wisp of smoke and a cocoa finish.
data.spiritLine: Rested tequila gives it body; the half ounce of mezcal adds the smoke.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Oaxaca Old Fashioned swaps the whiskey for tequila and a touch of smoky mezcal.”
data.story: Created in 2007 by Phil Ward at Death & Co. in New York. His original used aromatic bitters; chocolate bitters are common now.

video.title: The Oaxaca Old Fashioned - as if the old fashioned couldn't get any cooler · Anders Erickson

data.name: Mint Julep
data.description: Bourbon, mint and a little sugar, stirred over crushed ice in a frosty metal cup. The Kentucky Derby drink.
steps: Gently press the mint with the sugar and water in the cup.
Fill with crushed ice.
Add the bourbon and stir until the cup frosts.
Top with more ice and a mint sprig.
data.tasteLine: Ice-cold bourbon with fresh mint. Strong, but goes down easy.

riffs.name: Mojito
riffs.note: Rum, lime and mint, with soda.

riffs.name: Southside
riffs.note: Gin, lemon and mint, served up.

data.spiritLine: A higher-proof bourbon holds up as the crushed ice melts.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Mint Julep is bourbon, fresh mint and a little sugar over crushed ice: the Kentucky Derby drink.”
data.story: It began in the American South, with the earliest known mentions from 1770 in Virginia. Churchill Downs has paired it with the Kentucky Derby since 1938.

video.title: TWO Mint Juleps! - the bourbon & prescription julep · Anders Erickson

data.name: Bee’s Knees
data.description: Gin shaken with honey and fresh citrus, served up. Bright, floral and easy to like.
steps: Stir the honey syrup into the juices until it dissolves.
Add the gin and shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Garnish with a citrus zest.
data.tasteLine: Tart and floral, with soft honey sweetness.
data.spiritLine: A London dry gin keeps it crisp against the honey.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Bee’s Knees is gin with honey and fresh lemon, shaken and served up. Bright and floral.”
data.story: Long thought to be a Prohibition drink, it was first credited in Paris: the 1929 book Cocktails de Paris names Frank Meier of the Hôtel Ritz. The orange juice comes from David Embury’s 1948 version, which IBA follows.

video.title: Master The Classics: Bee's Knees · The Educated Barfly

data.name: Corpse Reviver No. 2
data.tagline: Equal parts, with a hint of absinthe
data.description: Gin, orange liqueur, Lillet Blanc and lemon in equal parts, with a dash of absinthe. Bright, tart and crisp.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with orange zest.
data.tasteLine: Zesty and dry, with a whisper of anise.
data.spiritLine: Gin is the backbone; the absinthe should be barely there.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Corpse Reviver No. 2 is equal parts gin, orange liqueur, Lillet and lemon, with a touch of absinthe.”
data.story: From Harry Craddock’s Savoy Cocktail Book (1930), written at the Savoy’s American Bar in London. Craddock warned that “four of these taken in swift succession will unrevive the corpse again.”

video.title: Gin Cocktail Recipe - The Corpse Reviver #2 · Anders Erickson

data.name: Aviation
data.description: Gin, maraschino, lemon and a touch of crème de violette, shaken and served up. Pale sky-blue to violet.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Add a cherry if you like.
data.tasteLine: Floral and tart, with a light cherry note.
data.spiritLine: A classic London dry gin keeps the violet from tasting soapy.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Aviation is gin, lemon, maraschino and a little violet liqueur. Floral and tart, pale violet in color.”
data.story: Created by Hugo Ensslin, head bartender at the Hotel Wallick in New York, and printed in his 1916 book. The 1930 Savoy Cocktail Book left out the crème de violette, and many bars followed for decades.

video.title: How to Make the Best Aviation Cocktail - shaken or stirred? · Anders Erickson

data.name: Clover Club
data.tagline: Gin, raspberry and a silky foam
data.description: Gin, raspberry and lemon shaken with egg white, served up with a pink foam.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake hard with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with raspberries.
data.tasteLine: Tart raspberry with a soft, silky foam.
data.spiritLine: Gin keeps the raspberry from tasting like candy.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Clover Club is gin, raspberry and lemon, shaken with egg white for a silky pink foam.”
data.story: A pre-Prohibition drink named for the Clover Club, a Philadelphia men’s club that met at the Bellevue-Stratford Hotel. It first appears under this name in a 1910 bar manual.

video.title: Clover Club Gin Cocktail Recipe · Steve the Bartender

data.allergyNote: Egg white is raw. Ask every guest, and note it on the ticket.

data.name: Naked and Famous
data.description: Mezcal, Yellow Chartreuse, Aperol and lime in equal parts, shaken and served up.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
data.tasteLine: Smoky, herbal and bittersweet, balanced by lime.
data.spiritLine: An espadín mezcal brings the smoke without taking over.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “Naked and Famous is equal parts mezcal, Yellow Chartreuse, Aperol and lime. Smoky, herbal and bright.”
data.story: Created by Joaquín Simó at Death & Co in New York in 2011, crossing the Last Word with the Paper Plane. The IBA added it to its official list in 2020.

video.title: Let's get Naked and Famous · The Educated Barfly

data.name: Gold Rush
data.description: A whiskey sour made with honey instead of sugar. Bourbon, lemon and honey syrup, shaken and served on the rocks.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake hard with ice.
Strain over fresh ice in a rocks glass.
Garnish with a lemon wedge.
data.tasteLine: Smooth and tart, with warm honey.

riffs.name: Whiskey Sour
riffs.note: Sugar instead of honey, with egg white.

data.spiritLine: Bourbon’s vanilla and caramel go well with honey.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Gold Rush is a whiskey sour made with honey: bourbon, lemon and honey over ice.”
data.story: Thought up by T. J. Siegel in 2001 at Milk & Honey in New York, where Sasha Petraske first made it.

video.title: Gold Rush 2 Ways Plus An Easy Hack For Your Sours · The Educated Barfly

data.name: Hemingway Daiquiri
data.description: A dry, tart daiquiri with grapefruit and maraschino. No added sugar.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
data.tasteLine: Tart and dry, with grapefruit up front.
data.spiritLine: A light rum keeps it crisp. There’s no sugar, so the rum has to be smooth.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Hemingway Daiquiri is rum, lime, grapefruit and maraschino. Drier and more tart than a classic daiquiri.”
data.story: Made at El Floridita in Havana for Ernest Hemingway, who wanted his daiquiri with no sugar and double rum. A later head bartender added the grapefruit and maraschino. IBA lists it as the Hemingway Special.

video.title: The one and only HEMINGWAY daiquiri · Anders Erickson

data.name: Southside
data.description: Gin, fresh citrus, sugar and mint, shaken and served up. Like a gin mojito without the soda.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake well with ice.
Double strain into a chilled coupe.
Garnish with mint.
data.tasteLine: Fresh, minty and bright.

riffs.name: Mojito
riffs.note: Rum, lime and mint, with soda.

data.spiritLine: A London dry gin. IBA uses lemon; many bars use lime, so check our build.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Southside is gin, citrus and fresh mint, shaken and served up. Like a gin mojito without the bubbles.”
data.story: Its origin is uncertain. The name may come from Chicago’s South Side, or from the Southside Sportsmen’s Club on Long Island.

video.title: How to Make a Southside Cocktail | Classic Gin Drink · Anders Erickson

data.name: Bramble
data.description: A gin sour over crushed ice, with blackberry liqueur drizzled over the top so it bleeds down through the drink.
steps: Shake gin, lemon and syrup with ice.
Strain over crushed ice in a rocks glass.
Drizzle the blackberry liqueur over the top in a circle.
Garnish with blackberries and lemon.
data.tasteLine: Tart lemon up top, sweet blackberry as it bleeds through.

riffs.name: Gin Fizz
riffs.note: A gin sour lengthened with soda.

data.spiritLine: London dry gin keeps it sharp under the berry.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Bramble is gin and lemon over crushed ice, with blackberry liqueur drizzled on top.”
data.story: Created in the mid-1980s by Dick Bradsell at Fred’s Club in Soho, London.

video.title: How to make the Bramble - an easy gin drink! · Anders Erickson

data.name: Old Cuban
data.description: Aged rum, lime, mint and bitters shaken and served up, then topped with Champagne.
steps: Add everything except the sparkling wine to a shaker.
Shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled coupe.
Top with the sparkling wine and garnish with mint.
data.tasteLine: Fresh and bubbly, with warm rum and spice underneath.

riffs.name: Mojito
riffs.note: White rum, mint and soda, tall.

data.spiritLine: An aged rum gives it depth under the mint and bubbles.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Old Cuban is like a mojito made with aged rum, served up and topped with Champagne.”
data.story: Created by Audrey Saunders in New York in the early 2000s. Sources disagree on the year: 2001 or 2004.

video.title: What if the Mojito became a Champagne Cocktail...? The Old Cuban · The Educated Barfly

data.name: Tom Collins
data.description: Gin, fresh lemon and sugar, topped with soda over ice. Tall, tart and refreshing.
steps: Fill the glass with ice.
Add gin, lemon and syrup.
Top with soda and stir gently.
Garnish with a lemon slice and a cherry.
data.tasteLine: Like a sparkling gin lemonade.
data.spiritLine: Old Tom is a slightly sweeter gin. With London dry, it’s a John Collins.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Tom Collins is gin, fresh lemon and a little sugar, topped with soda. Like a sparkling gin lemonade.”
data.story: The first published recipe is in Harry Johnson’s 1882 bar manual. The name is disputed: it may come from an 1874 New York hoax (“Have you seen Tom Collins?”) or from the older John Collins of London.

video.title: Beat the heat with the TOM COLLINS - an easy gin drink! · Anders Erickson

data.name: Gin Fizz
data.tagline: Gin, lemon and a splash of soda
data.description: Gin, lemon and sugar shaken hard and lengthened with a splash of soda. Served without ice.
steps: Shake gin, lemon and syrup with ice.
Strain into a chilled glass with no ice.
Top with a splash of soda.
Garnish with a lemon slice.
data.tasteLine: Crisp and lively, lighter than a Collins.

riffs.name: Ramos Gin Fizz
riffs.note: Adds cream, egg white and orange flower water.

data.spiritLine: A London dry gin. Shake it hard: the fizz comes from both the shake and the soda.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Gin Fizz is gin, lemon and sugar shaken and topped with soda, served without ice.”
data.story: A mid-1800s classic, printed in Jerry Thomas’s 1876 Bar-tenders Guide. Fizzes were hugely popular in America from 1900 to the 1940s, especially in New Orleans.

video.title: Gin Fizz classic recipe · The Educated Barfly

data.name: Ramos Gin Fizz
data.description: Gin, citrus, cream, egg white and orange flower water, shaken for a long time and topped with soda. Light, creamy and tall.
steps: Shake everything except the soda with ice for about two minutes.
Strain, then shake again without ice for one minute.
Pour into a chilled glass.
Top slowly with soda so the foam rises.
data.tasteLine: Light and creamy, like a citrus cloud.
data.spiritLine: Old Tom or London dry. The work here is the shake, not the spirit.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Ramos Gin Fizz is a New Orleans classic: gin, citrus, cream and egg white, shaken a long time. Light and creamy. It takes a few extra minutes.”
data.story: Created in 1888 by Henry C. Ramos in New Orleans. IBA says his bar kept a line of bartenders shaking it in relay. Sources disagree on which of his bars came first.

video.title: Easy and perfect Ramos Gin Fizz · The Educated Barfly

data.allergyNote: Egg white is raw, and there’s cream. Ask every guest, and note it on the ticket.

data.name: Dark ’n’ Stormy
data.description: Ginger beer over ice with dark rum floated on top, so it looks like a storm cloud. Bermuda’s national drink.
steps: Fill a highball with ice.
Pour in the ginger beer.
Float the rum on top. Don’t stir.
Garnish with lime.
data.tasteLine: Spicy ginger with rich, dark rum.
data.spiritLine: “Dark ’n Stormy” is a Gosling’s trademark, and the official build uses Gosling’s Black Seal.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Dark ’n’ Stormy is ginger beer with dark rum floated on top, and a wedge of lime.”
data.story: Called the national drink of Bermuda, where Gosling’s rum is made. Who made it first is unknown; the legend is British sailors on shore leave after World War I.

video.title: How to Make the Dark 'N Stormy - get it right · Anders Erickson

data.name: Tequila Sunrise
data.description: Tequila and orange juice over ice, with grenadine sunk to the bottom for a sunrise look.
steps: Fill a highball with ice.
Add tequila and orange juice.
Pour the grenadine in so it sinks. Don’t stir.
Garnish with an orange slice.
data.tasteLine: Sweet and fruity, like tequila orange juice.
data.spiritLine: A blanco tequila keeps it bright.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Tequila Sunrise is tequila and orange juice with grenadine sunk to the bottom, like a sunrise.”
data.story: The modern version was created around 1970 by Bobby Lozoff at the Trident in Sausalito, California, and spread after the Rolling Stones drank it on their 1972 tour. A different 1930s Tequila Sunrise came from the Arizona Biltmore.

video.title: The Tequila Sunrise - which one is better? · Anders Erickson

data.name: Long Island Iced Tea
data.description: Vodka, tequila, rum, gin and orange liqueur with lemon and sugar, topped with cola. Tastes like iced tea, but very strong.
steps: Fill a highball with ice.
Add the spirits, lemon and syrup.
Top with a splash of cola and stir gently.
Garnish with a lemon slice.
data.tasteLine: Sweet and citrusy. It hides how strong it is.

riffs.name: Tokyo Tea
riffs.note: Melon liqueur instead of orange liqueur, topped with lemon-lime soda.

data.spiritLine: Half an ounce each of four spirits plus orange liqueur. That’s about two and a half ounces of alcohol, so pace it.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Long Island has vodka, tequila, rum, gin and orange liqueur with lemon and a splash of cola. No tea, and it’s strong.”
data.story: Robert “Rosebud” Butt says he invented it in 1972 for a contest at the Oak Beach Inn on Long Island, New York. A rival story places it in 1920s Long Island, Tennessee.

video.title: Make the Best EVER Long Island Iced Tea · Anders Erickson

data.name: Americano
data.description: Campari and sweet vermouth over ice with a splash of soda. Bitter, light and low in alcohol.
steps: Fill the glass with ice.
Add Campari and vermouth.
Top with a splash of soda and stir gently.
Garnish with a half orange slice.
data.tasteLine: Bittersweet and refreshing, lighter than a Negroni.
data.spiritLine: Campari leads. IBA serves it in a rocks glass; many bars serve it long in a Collins.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “An Americano is Campari and sweet vermouth with soda. Like a lighter Negroni.”
data.story: First served at Gaspare Campari’s café in Milan in the 1860s, as a longer version of the Milano-Torino. Difford’s says the name means “American-style,” from vermouth with bitters added.

video.title: The Negroni and the Americano | easy cocktails with Campari! · Anders Erickson

data.name: Kir Royale
data.description: A little blackcurrant liqueur topped with Champagne. Pink, dry and elegant.
steps: Pour the cassis into a flute.
Top slowly with Champagne.
data.tasteLine: Dry bubbles with a soft blackcurrant note.
data.spiritLine: Champagne makes it a Kir Royale. With another sparkling wine, it’s often called a Kir Pétillant.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Kir Royale is Champagne with a little blackcurrant liqueur.”
data.story: The sparkling version of the Kir, from Dijon in France. The Kir is named after Canon Félix Kir, the mayor of Dijon who promoted it after World War II.

video.title: Kir Royale Champagne Cocktail | Joel Fraser · Jamie Oliver - Drinks

data.name: Mai Tai
data.description: Two rums, fresh lime, orange curaçao and almond orgeat, shaken and poured over ice. The tiki classic.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake with ice.
Pour into the glass.
Garnish with pineapple, mint and lime peel.
data.tasteLine: Rich rum, tart lime and nutty almond. Not as sweet as people expect.
data.spiritLine: Two rums: a funky Jamaican and a Martinique rum. IBA notes Trader Vic’s Martinique rum was made from molasses.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Mai Tai is two rums with fresh lime, orange curaçao and almond syrup. Tart and nutty. It contains almond.”
data.story: Trader Vic said he invented it in 1944 at his bar in Oakland, California. Donn Beach (Don the Beachcomber) claimed he made it first, in 1933.

video.title: How to Make a Mai Tai | a very tasty tiki recipe! · Anders Erickson

data.allergyNote: Orgeat is almond syrup. Tell guests with a nut allergy.

data.name: Piña Colada
data.description: White rum, coconut cream and pineapple juice, blended with ice. Creamy, sweet and tropical.
steps: Add everything to a blender with ice.
Blend until smooth.
Pour into the glass.
Garnish with pineapple and a cherry, and add a straw.
data.tasteLine: Creamy, sweet and tropical, like a vacation.

riffs.name: Painkiller
riffs.note: Dark rum, orange juice and nutmeg.

data.spiritLine: A light rum lets the coconut and pineapple shine.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Piña Colada is white rum, coconut cream and pineapple, blended with ice.”
data.story: The Caribe Hilton in San Juan credits bartender Ramón “Monchito” Marrero with creating it in 1954, though others at the hotel and nearby claim it too. Puerto Rico made it the official drink in 1978.

video.title: PIÑA COLADA - the ultimate vacation drink! · Anders Erickson

data.allergyNote: Coconut cream. Some guests with tree-nut allergies avoid coconut, so ask.

data.name: Jungle Bird
data.description: Dark rum, Campari, pineapple and lime, shaken and served over ice. Tropical with a bitter edge.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake with ice.
Strain into a glass filled with ice.
Garnish with a pineapple wedge.
data.tasteLine: Juicy pineapple with a bitter, dark finish.
data.spiritLine: Blackstrap rum is dark and molasses-heavy, which stands up to the Campari.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “The Jungle Bird is dark rum, Campari, pineapple and lime. Tropical, with a bitter edge.”
data.story: Created by Jeffrey Ong at the Aviary Bar in the Kuala Lumpur Hilton, where it was the welcome drink from 1973. Today’s version, with blackstrap rum and less pineapple, comes from Giuseppe González in New York in 2010.

video.title: The JUNGLE BIRD - history & recipe of this juicy tropical classic! · Anders Erickson

data.name: Caipirinha
data.description: Cachaça, fresh lime and sugar, muddled and served over cracked ice.
steps: Gently muddle the lime and sugar in the glass.
Fill with cracked ice.
Add the cachaça.
Stir gently.
data.tasteLine: Bright lime with a grassy, sugarcane bite.
data.spiritLine: Cachaça is Brazil’s sugarcane spirit, made from fresh cane juice. It’s grassier than most rum.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Caipirinha is Brazil’s national cocktail: cachaça, fresh lime and sugar over ice.”
data.story: The name means “little country girl.” It came from the countryside of São Paulo state, Brazil. One story says it grew out of a Spanish flu remedy of cachaça, lime, honey and garlic.

video.title: The Caipirinha - what to drink when it's hot! · Anders Erickson

data.name: Bloody Mary
data.description: Vodka and tomato juice with lemon, Worcestershire, hot sauce, celery salt and pepper. The brunch classic.
data.ice: None, or cubes in a highball if asked
steps: Add everything to a mixing glass with ice.
Stir gently.
Pour into the glass (over ice in a highball if the guest asks).
Garnish with celery and a lemon wedge.
data.tasteLine: Savory and spicy, like a peppery tomato juice with a kick.
data.spiritLine: Vodka stays in the background so the spice does the talking.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Bloody Mary is vodka and tomato juice with lemon, Worcestershire and spice. How spicy would you like it?”
data.story: Fernand Petiot is said to have created it at Harry’s New York Bar in Paris in 1921, then refined it at the St. Regis in New York. New York’s 21 Club credits comedian George Jessel instead.

video.title: How to make a Bloody Mary (from scratch) · Anders Erickson

data.allergyNote: Most Worcestershire sauce contains anchovy. Check our bottle and tell guests with a fish allergy.

data.name: Mimosa
data.description: Equal parts fresh orange juice and sparkling wine in a flute.
steps: Pour the orange juice into a flute.
Top gently with sparkling wine.
Stir once, gently.
data.tasteLine: Fresh orange juice with bubbles. Light and easy.

riffs.name: Bellini
riffs.note: Peach purée instead of orange juice.

data.spiritLine: IBA uses Prosecco. Many bars use Champagne or cava; ask what we pour.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Mimosa is fresh orange juice and sparkling wine.”
data.story: Its origin is unclear; it was first called a “champagne orange.” The Paris Ritz’s Frank Meier is sometimes credited. It’s close kin to the Buck’s Fizz, from about 1921.

video.title: How to Make the Best Mimosa | Julia At Home (S5 E2) · America's Test Kitchen

data.name: Bellini
data.description: White peach purée topped with Prosecco. Venice’s famous brunch drink.
steps: Add the peach purée to a mixing glass with ice.
Add the Prosecco and stir gently.
Pour into a chilled flute.
data.tasteLine: Soft, ripe peach with gentle bubbles.
data.spiritLine: Prosecco’s soft fruit matches the peach.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Bellini is white peach purée topped with Prosecco.”
data.story: Created by Giuseppe Cipriani at Harry’s Bar in Venice in 1945, and named after the painter Giovanni Bellini for its pink color.

video.title: There's Nothing Better Than A Fresh Fruit Bellini · The Educated Barfly

data.name: Irish Coffee
data.description: Hot coffee, Irish whiskey and sugar, with a layer of cold cream floated on top. Drink it through the cream.
steps: Warm the glass with hot water, then empty it.
Add hot coffee, whiskey and sugar, and stir until dissolved.
Lightly whip the cream.
Float it on top over the back of a spoon. Don’t stir.
data.tasteLine: Hot, sweet coffee and whiskey through a cold layer of cream.

riffs.name: Hot Toddy
riffs.note: Whiskey, honey, lemon and hot water.

data.spiritLine: A smooth blended Irish whiskey is the classic choice.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “An Irish Coffee is hot coffee with Irish whiskey and a little sugar, topped with cold cream.”
data.story: Joe Sheridan, chef at the Foynes air base near today’s Shannon Airport, is credited with adding whiskey to arriving passengers’ coffee in the early 1940s. A newspaper writer brought it to San Francisco’s Buena Vista Cafe in 1952.

video.title: Irish Coffee - hot AND cold 🔥🧊 · Anders Erickson

data.name: Hot Toddy
data.tagline: Whiskey, honey, lemon and hot water
data.description: Whiskey, honey and lemon topped with hot water, with cloves. A warm, soothing nightcap.
steps: Warm the glass with hot water, then empty it.
Add whiskey, lemon, honey and syrup, then the cloves.
Top with boiling water and stir.
Garnish with a lemon slice and a cinnamon stick.
data.tasteLine: Warm, soft and soothing, with honey and spice.
data.spiritLine: Scotch, bourbon, rum or brandy all work. Ask the guest.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Hot Toddy is whiskey with honey, lemon and hot water. Any whiskey you prefer?”
data.story: The word comes from the Indian “toddy,” a palm drink. Difford’s finds the first toddy reference in 1741; Wikipedia dates the hot spirit drink to 1786. A Whisky Toddy is in Jerry Thomas’s 1862 guide.

video.title: 3 Hot Toddy Recipes - Scotch, Rum, & Mezcal! · Anders Erickson

data.name: White Russian
data.description: Vodka and coffee liqueur over ice with cream floated on top. Sweet, creamy and strong.
steps: Stir vodka and coffee liqueur with ice.
Strain into a rocks glass filled with ice.
Lightly shake or whip the cream.
Float it on top and grate nutmeg over it.
data.tasteLine: Like an iced coffee with cream, and a kick.

riffs.name: Black Russian
riffs.note: Vodka and coffee liqueur, no cream.

riffs.name: Espresso Martini
riffs.note: Vodka, coffee liqueur and espresso, shaken.

data.spiritLine: Vodka keeps it clean so the coffee and cream lead.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A White Russian is vodka and coffee liqueur over ice with cream on top.”
data.story: It’s the Black Russian (from 1949) with cream added. It first appeared in print in 1965 and became hugely popular after the film The Big Lebowski (1998).

video.title: The White Russian - history, recipe, & taste off! · Anders Erickson

data.name: Brandy Alexander
data.description: Cognac, crème de cacao and cream, shaken and served up with nutmeg. A dessert in a glass.
steps: Add everything to a shaker.
Shake with ice.
Strain into a chilled glass.
Grate nutmeg over the top.
data.tasteLine: Rich and creamy, like a boozy chocolate milkshake.
data.spiritLine: Cognac adds warmth and fruit under the chocolate.
data.pour: Bar lead to add our bottle
data.say: “A Brandy Alexander is cognac, chocolate liqueur and cream, shaken, with nutmeg on top. Like dessert.”
data.story: The original Alexander was made with gin. Harry MacElhone, then at Ciro’s in London, is credited with switching to brandy; the first brandy recipe is in his 1923 book.

video.title: The Brandy Alexander - a simple holiday drink · Anders Erickson
